transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess what finally made me come in is that things at work got… kind of out of hand. I’m an industrial production manager, so I’m used to juggling a lot, and I normally like being the person who can keep the plant moving. But recently I went from just doing my regular job to launching redesign projects one after another — like nonstop — changing layouts, rethinking workflows, calling suppliers after hours because I’d suddenly have another idea, rewriting the shift plan myself instead of delegating it.

At the time it felt like I was just being productive, like I could see all these improvements nobody else was moving fast enough on. But then it all caught up with me. I had set so many things in motion that suddenly I couldn’t keep up with my own plans. People were asking me for decisions and updates on things I had started, and I just… couldn’t stay on top of it anymore. That swing from pushing everything forward to being overwhelmed by the mess I created is what scared me enough to come here.
Can you describe how you were feeling emotionally during that time when you were launching all these projects and working so intensively?

At first, honestly, I felt… almost electrically upbeat. Like there was this current running through me, and everything seemed possible and urgent in a good way. I remember feeling like I could look at the whole plant and suddenly see exactly what needed to be fixed, like it was all obvious and everyone else had just been moving too slowly or thinking too small.

But it wasn’t just “happy,” exactly. It was more intense than that. I felt excited, driven, kind of lit up from the inside. And then pretty quickly, if someone questioned one of my ideas or asked if we should slow down or review the cost first, I’d get weirdly irritated. Not just normal workplace frustration — it felt personal, like they were blocking something important that I could see so clearly. I’d think, “Why are you dragging your feet? This is obvious.” 

Looking back, that irritability stands out because I’m used to pushback at work. That’s part of the job. But during that time it felt unbearable, like any hesitation from other people was getting in the way of momentum I felt we absolutely had to act on.
During that time when you felt so driven and excited, did you feel like your mood was unusually high or irritable for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a week?

Yes… I mean, yes, it really did feel unusually high for me, especially at the beginning of that assignment. It wasn’t just that I was motivated or having a good stretch at work. I felt almost electrically upbeat, like my mind was constantly connecting things and every idea felt urgent and important.

And then alongside that, or maybe after it started building, I became really irritable in this way that doesn’t feel like my normal work stress. If anyone questioned my ideas or wanted to slow down and review something, I felt like they were dragging everything down — like they were slowing down something that was completely obvious and important to me. It felt intensely frustrating, more than the situation really called for.

I’m not sure I can neatly measure it the way you’re asking, like “most of the day” or “nearly every day,” but it definitely wasn’t just a quick mood. It was the overall tone of that period — very up, very driven, and then easily irritated when people didn’t move with me.

latest_inference.note: The patient described a distinct period of abnormally elevated and irritable mood, increased goal-directed activity, and impaired judgment or insight, which aligns with a manic episode. The duration and intensity of symptoms, along with the resulting impairment, support a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder, current episode manic, mild. Other candidates (F30.1, F32.1, F31.3) are ruled out based on the presence of a full manic episode without indication of major depressive episodes occurring concurrently or exclusively.
